presentingComplaint: Sudden-onset severe, diffuse abdominal pain for 5 hours with associated palpitations and one episode of bloody stool.
history: 74-year-old man with longstanding hypertension and paroxysmal atrial fibrillation (poorly compliant with apixaban, self-discontinued 3 weeks ago citing bruising). Woke with abrupt, agonising, generalised colicky abdominal pain reaching maximal intensity within minutes. Pain has been unremitting and disproportionate to a soft, only mildly tender abdomen. He has vomited twice and passed one loose maroon-coloured stool. Simultaneously he became aware of rapid palpitations and mild central chest tightness, prompting the ED to activate a chest-pain pathway - raising acute coronary syndrome and rapid AF as the overlapping emergency. No prior similar pain; reports several months of vague post-prandial abdominal discomfort and food fear with 4 kg weight loss (intestinal angina). Ex-smoker, known peripheral vascular disease.
examination: Distressed, restless with pain markedly out of proportion to physical findings. Abdomen soft, mildly distended, generalised tenderness without guarding or rebound early on; bowel sounds reduced. Irregularly irregular pulse. No pulsatile mass. Peripheries cool, mottled. Rectal exam: dark blood on glove. Chest clear; no basal crackles.
imaging: ECG: atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response ~125/min, no acute ST-elevation, minor rate-related non-specific T-wave changes. Erect chest X-ray: no free air, no consolidation. CT angiography (arterial + portal venous phase) of abdomen/pelvis: abrupt filling defect in the proximal superior mesenteric artery ~3 cm from origin with non-opacification of distal branches; segmental small-bowel wall thinning and poor mural enhancement of mid-jejunum/ileum; no pneumatosis or portal venous gas yet; no AAA, normal pancreas, no obstruction/transition point.
microbiology: Not applicable to the primary diagnosis. Blood cultures sent as part of the sepsis/acidosis screen pending; no source of infection identified.
differentialDiagnoses: Acute mesenteric ischemia (SMA embolism from AF) - final diagnosis
Acute coronary syndrome / rapid AF (overlapping emergency raised by chest tightness + troponin rise)
finalDiagnosis: Acute arterial (embolic) mesenteric ischemia - SMA embolus secondary to atrial fibrillation, with early lactic acidosis; concurrent rapid AF and a modest troponin rise (demand ischemia) constituting the overlapping emergency.
citations: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22e - Mesenteric Vascular Insufficiency / Acute Intestinal Ischemia
World Society of Emergency Surgery (WSES) - Acute Mesenteric Ischemia guidelines 2017
AHA/ACC - Peripheral Artery / Mesenteric Ischemia management (mesenteric arterial disease) 2016
stewardship: Not applicable as a primary infective indication - acute mesenteric ischemia is a non-infective vascular emergency and empirical antibiotics do not treat the underlying diagnosis. Management is time-critical revascularisation (emergency angiography/embolectomy or endovascular therapy), systemic anticoagulation, fluid resuscitation and urgent surgical review; broad-spectrum antibiotics are given only peri-operatively/if transmural infarction, perforation or resection occurs (source-driven), not as treatment of the ischemia itself. Avoid vasoconstrictors where possible.
contraindications: Avoid alpha-agonist / high-dose vasoconstrictor pressors where feasible - worsen mesenteric hypoperfusion.
Do not delay CT angiography or surgical/vascular consult for observation - infarction is time-dependent.
Withhold nephrotoxins and dose-adjust for creatinine 1.6; use iso-osmolar contrast cautiously but do NOT omit CTA.
Avoid digoxin as sole rate control in hypotension; treat the ischemic driver rather than reflexively rate-controlling AF.
edgeCases: Soft, unremarkable abdomen with pain out of proportion is the classic early trap - normal exam does NOT exclude ischemia.
Absence of pneumatosis/portal venous gas is EARLY disease, not exclusion; do not falsely reassure.
Troponin rise and chest tightness can misdirect to ACS; the pain-out-of-proportion + AF + lactate points to mesenteric embolism.
Normal lactate early does not exclude AMI; a rising lactate signals transmural infarction.
expectedMaiK: Sudden severe abdominal pain out of proportion to exam in an elderly patient with atrial fibrillation and elevated lactate is embolic acute mesenteric ischemia until proven otherwise - obtain immediate CT angiography and emergency vascular/surgical revascularisation; the coexisting rapid AF and troponin rise are the overlapping emergency, not the primary cause.
expectedNextQuestions: Onset and character of the pain (sudden vs gradual) and whether it is out of proportion to examination?
History of atrial fibrillation, anticoagulation adherence, or prior embolic events?
Any preceding post-prandial pain, food fear or weight loss (chronic mesenteric ischemia)?
Blood in stool or vomit, and time since last normal bowel function?
